claims.text: This tour spans 3 km along the waterfront, from Union Oyster House, founded in 1826, to The Barking Crab.
Immerse yourself in Boston's seafood legacy, where Union Oyster House, the city's oldest restaurant, stands as a testament to 200 years of history.
Legal Sea Foods - Long Wharf, with its commitment to sustainable fishing, and The Capital Grille, renowned for dry-aged steaks, add modern flair to this culinary narrative.
Explore how Boston's culinary landscape blends tradition and innovation through these storied establishments.
At Union Oyster House, you'll encounter the simple wooden booth.
Walk northwest on Union St, notice the cobblestone streets and historic buildings.
You're standing at the threshold of the Union Oyster House, Boston's oldest continuously operating restaurant, open since 1826.
Inside the Union Oyster House, booths and corners hold tales of its illustrious past.

Daniel Webster, a prominent 19th-century American statesman, consumed at least six tall tumblers of brandy and water alongside half a dozen plates of raw oysters here, cementing the restaurant's status as a staple in Boston’s culinary heritage.
The Union Oyster House has a rich history involving John F. Kennedy, the 35th President of the United States.
Booth #18 is now permanently dedicated to his memory, providing a tangible connection to one of the most memorable leaders.
Beyond its historical anecdotes, the Union Oyster House offers a taste of tradition with its Yankee-style seafood.
If you're in the mood for fresh New England lobster or a hearty plate of grilled meats, this is the place to be.
The cost averages between $35 and $45 per person for a casual lunch, with entrees priced around $25.95 to $34.95.
Look towards Legal Sea Foods, a fixture in Boston's culinary scene, where tradition meets modernity.

Known for its New England clam chowder, which has been a staple at every presidential inauguration since Ronald Reagan's in 1981, it embodies a commitment to quality that has elevated it to iconic status.
The chowder, rich and creamy, exemplifies the flavors of New England, and it's served alongside other seafood delights like lobster rolls and crab cakes.
In January 1980, a three-alarm fire consumed the original Legal Sea Foods location in Cambridge on the very day the owners were celebrating their expansion into Boston.
This unexpected catastrophe might have spelled the end for some, but for Legal Sea Foods, it marked a new beginning.
This resilience is mirrored in the bustling atmosphere of the Long Wharf location, where every dish served is a nod to the history and commitment that the restaurant embodies.
The location at Long Wharf is steeped in history, connecting today's diners with Boston's vibrant past.
In 1854, this area found itself at the heart of a contentious moment in American history.
Anthony Burns, a fugitive slave, was captured by federal marshals in Boston, sparking abolitionist riots that highlighted the city's role in the national debate over slavery.
His forced return to the South under President Franklin Pierce's orders stirred public outcry and fueled the abolitionist movement, illustrating Boston's complex history of progress and struggle.

When visiting Legal Sea Foods - Long Wharf, you're stepping into a narrative that spans centuries, from the tumultuous events of the 18th and 19th centuries to the modern-day commitment to culinary excellence.
Open daily from 11:00 am, with extended hours on weekends, this establishment invites you to savor not just the food but the enduring stories that make Boston unique.
Look around and note how the bustling atmosphere from the stop at Legal Sea Foods seems to follow us here, adding a layer of vibrant energy and setting the stage for moments of indulgence.
Step into The Capital Grille, a name that resonates with luxury and exclusivity.
This is not merely a place to dine; it's a grand example of Boston's luxurious culinary culture.
Known for its historical location, the original Boston site became legendary during the 1990s and 2000s for its distinctive "private wine locker" culture.
claims.evidence: The original Boston location of The Capital Grille became legendary during the 1990s and 2000s for its VIP power-broker 'private wine locker' culture.

claims.text: Now, let me tell you about a slice of the Capital Grille's contemporary story that isn’t highlighted on the menu.
In one of the more dramatic chapters for its parent company, Darden Restaurants, they faced a federal class-action lawsuit for wage theft and racial discrimination.
claims.evidence: The Capital Grille's parent company was involved in a federal class-action lawsuit for wage theft and racial discrimination, resulting in millions of dollars in settlements.

claims.text: Back in the present day, the Capital Grille in Boston hosts more than just steak aficionados.

At this upscale dining spot, sightings of both local and rival NBA stars have become the stuff of legend, with pro athletes including Celtics and Bruins players often seen enjoying the extensive wine list.
This prestigious spot invites advance reservations and offers entrées starting around $42 to $47, with a tempting three-course dinner menu priced at $55.
You’ll find doors open to this opulent world from 11:30 am to 10 pm on weekdays, slightly narrower on Sunday, but extended until 11 pm on Friday and Saturday.
After so much exclusivity and hidden tales, prepare yourself for a contrasting end to our journey, where rustic charm meets Boston’s vibrant atmosphere just up ahead.
Set against the backdrop of Boston's bustling Seaport District, this lively seafood shack invites you into its world of hearty maritime fare and local camaraderie.
The Barking Crab first opened its doors in May 1994, under the name 'Venus — Seafood in the Rough'.
claims.evidence: The Barking Crab opened in May 1994 as a seasonal pop-up shack called 'Venus — Seafood in the Rough'.

claims.text: Originally conceived as a seasonal pop-up, this quirky shack quickly became a staple of Boston's waterfront dining scene.
In the mid-2000s, the restaurant faced a pivotal moment when Boston developer John B. Hynes III proposed moving The Barking Crab to make way for the 'Seaport Square' project.
claims.evidence: In March 2008, Boston developer John B. Hynes III proposed moving The Barking Crab for the 'Seaport Square' project, leading to a temporary city shutdown of the restaurant for sanitary violations.

claims.text: Another dramatic episode unfolded in July 2012, when the Boston Fire Department had to cut through the floorboards to extinguish a fire that had taken hold in the wooden pilings beneath the deck.
claims.evidence: In July 2012, the Boston Fire Department had to cut through The Barking Crab's floorboards to extinguish a fire burning within the wooden pilings underneath the deck.

claims.text: Open from Sunday to Wednesday from 12 to 9 pm and Thursday to Saturday until 10 pm, The Barking Crab does not take reservations, which means seating is first-come, first-served.
With a price range in the $$$ category, diners are treated to an authentic taste of Boston's seafood offerings.
